paper_title: PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Machine learning-based weather modeling has primarily developed along two paradigms: weather forecasting [14], which predicts future states at fixed spatial resolution, and weather downscaling [5 8], which refines either spatial resolution at fixed time or temporal resolution at fixed grid. These standard formulations typically emphasize subset of three axes: future prediction, spatial refinement, and temporal refinement. However, real-world applications that forecast high-resolution target from different, lower-resolution modality naturally involve all three axes. For example, minute-scale wind-power forecasting for renewable integration [9], sub-hourly precipitation nowcasting for floodrisk monitoring [10], and fine-scale aviation turbulence guidance for flight safety [11] all require future predictions at fine spatial and temporal resolution, regime that no prior work has explored. This raises natural question: Can single model jointly refine spatial and temporal resolution while extending predictions into the future? To answer this, we introduce Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), the task of mapping past low-resolution states to future high-resolution states, with resolution gaps in both space and time. PSWD formalizes joint spatiotemporal refinement and future prediction as unified learning task. It extends task-specific adaptation benchmarks for weather foundation models (WFMs) [12] to setting that requires all three capabilities jointly. PSWD requires model to infer fine-scale spatial structure and its evolution from the same coarse history. We address this task with scaffold-and-correct pipeline built around shared pretrained weather backbone. The spatial stage Corresponding author. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). predicts and refines high-resolution state at the final lead time. The temporal stage then uses this predicted endpoint and the upsampled present state to construct the target trajectory. Fixed spatial upsampling and temporal interpolation provide the scaffolds, while lightweight correction heads learn the residual details. In the scaffold-and-correct pipeline, the shared backbone provides the forecast that anchors both spatial and temporal refinement. To align this forecast with the final trajectory objective, we adapt the backbone jointly with the correction heads. Since the backbone already contains useful forecasting knowledge, this adaptation should build on its pretrained structure. At the same time, predicting high-resolution future trajectories may require corrections beyond the dominant pretrained directions. single low-rank update provides compact parameterization for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) [13], but it does not explicitly separate these two needs under fixed rank budget. This motivates an adaptation design that initializes one update path from the pretrained singular structure [14] while reserving another path for corrections outside the selected principal directions [15]. To this end, we propose PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), dual-branch low-rank adaptation method for the shared backbone. PROLA divides the fixed rank budget between principal branch initialized from dominant singular components and an orthogonal branch projected outside the selected principal subspaces. The principal factors remain freely trainable after initialization, while the orthogonal branch uses fixed projectors defined by the pretrained weight. Beyond this allocation, PROLA rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient-based branch and component scores, without increasing trainable rank. Branch scores adjust the relative update strength between the two paths, while component scores modulate individual updates within each path. Experiments on WeatherBench 2 [16] with the pretrained WFM backbone [4] show that PROLA improves over representative low-rank PEFT baselines under matched low-rank budgets for multivariable, multi-lead global weather downscaling. Ablations and diagnostics further support the scaffold-and-correct pipeline, the dual-branch design of PROLA, and gradient-guided scaling of optimizer updates. Together, these results support PSWD as challenging evaluation setting and PROLA as an effective adaptation method for pretrained weather backbones, with broader applicability across datasets and tasks. Our contributions are fourfold: We formulate Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD) to predict future high-resolution weather trajectories from recent coarse-resolution states, and introduce scaffold-and-correct pipeline to address it. We propose PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), low-rank PEFT method that allocates fixed rank budget between principal and orthogonal branches and rescales optimizer updates using gradient-based component scores. We show that PROLA outperforms representative PEFT baselines under matched low-rank budget and narrows the performance gap between low-rank PEFT and full fine-tuning in our PSWD setting. We demonstrate PROLAs effectiveness across datasets and the transferability of its adaptation design beyond weather downscaling.

sections.content: 5.1 Ablation of Scaffold-and-Correct Pipeline Table 4 compares direct prediction across PEFT methods and ablates the scaffold-and-correct pipeline with PROLA. Direct prediction jointly outputs all target lead times without the spatial-to-temporal decomposition. All pipeline ablations use PROLA and remove the spatial correction head Cs, the temporal correction head Ct, or both, leaving the corresponding scaffolds uncorrected. The full pipeline achieves the lowest RMSE across all five variables at 3h, reducing Z500 RMSE from 53.13 with direct prediction to 50.30. Removing both correction heads raises 3h Z500 RMSE to 87.73, indicating that the scaffolds alone are insufficient for PSWD. Removing Ct alone yields much higher 3h Z500 RMSE than removing Cs alone (84.53 vs. 53.35), highlighting the role of temporal correction at intermediate leads. sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Data-driven weather modeling. Data-driven weather forecasting has progressed from early global models [21, 22] to systems achieving competitive or state-of-the-art performance on global benchmarks [13, 16, 2326], alongside hybrid physics-ML and probabilistic systems [27, 28]. Weather downscaling reconstructs high-resolution fields from low-resolution inputs through spatial statistical or generative refinement [5, 8, 2933], with fewer studies addressing time-evolving or joint spatiotemporal refinement [7, 34, 35]. Pretrained weather foundation models (WFMs) support diverse atmospheric tasks [4, 3638], with their growing scale motivating PEFT [12]. Existing work often treats forecasting, spatial downscaling, temporal refinement, and WFM adaptation separately, whereas PSWD couples forecasting with spatiotemporal refinement in one objective and provides comprehensive PEFT benchmark for WFMs. Low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning. PEFT avoids costly full fine-tuning by adapting large pretrained backbones with few trainable parameters [39]. LoRA trains low-rank factors with frozen backbone [13]; variants add quantization, dynamic rank selection, parameter sharing, adaptive rank allocation, factor-wise learning rates, and magnitude-direction decomposition [17, 18, 4043]. Other methods use SVD/decomposition-based initialization [14, 44, 45] to exploit pretrained weight structure, or orthogonality constraints to reduce interference with pretrained or previously learned subspaces [15, 46, 47]. Related approaches distribute principal components across devices [48], restrict orthogonal transformations to selected subspaces [49, 50], or combine coefficient updates within fixed principal basis with orthogonal-complement adaptation [51]. PROLA splits fixed rank budget between principal and orthogonal branches, trains its principal factors, and scales optimizer updates using gradient-based branch and rank-1 component scores.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We formulated Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD) as predicting future highresolution global weather trajectories from recent coarse-resolution global states. We addressed PSWD with spatial-to-temporal scaffold-and-correct pipeline that reuses shared pretrained backbone and reconstructs target trajectories with fixed numerical scaffolds and lightweight residual heads. For parameter-efficient backbone adaptation, we proposed PROLA (Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which splits fixed rank budget across principal and orthogonal branches and rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals. Experiments show that PROLA outperforms low-rank PEFT baselines under matched low-rank budgets, indicating that preserving pretrained structure while reserving capacity for orthogonal corrections is effective for PSWD.

sections.title: C Detailed Experimental Setup
sections.content: For the main global PSWD experiments, we use Aurora [4] as the pretrained weather backbone, starting from the same pretrained checkpoint2 for all PEFT variants. The experiments use the WeatherBench 2 dataset3 [16] at two resolutions: 5.625 data available at 6-hour intervals for lowresolution inputs, and 1.5 data available at 1-hour intervals for high-resolution targets. The input lags are Hc = {0, δc} with δc = 6h. The target leads are Hf = {1h, . . . , 6h}, with δf = 1h and hend = 6h. The 5.625 inputs use 32 64 grid. sections.title: E Implementation Details
sections.content: The main Aurora training configuration uses two NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs. For PEFT and Head only experiments, we use per-GPU batch size 4 with gradient accumulation over 4 steps, giving an effective global batch size of 32. For Full FT, we use per-GPU batch size 2 with gradient accumulation over 8 steps, giving the same effective global batch size of 32. Models in this benchmark are trained for 10 epochs. We use AdamW [56] with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.999), ϵ = 108, and weight decay 0.05. The learning rate follows step-level cosine schedule with linear warmup. For PEFT and Head only experiments, the base learning rate is 5 104, the warmup learning rate is 106, the minimum learning rate is 106, and warmup lasts for one epoch. For Full FT, the backbone learning rate is 5 105, with warmup and minimum learning rates 107. The correction heads in Full FT use the learning rate 5 104. Gradient norm clipping is applied with maximum norm of 1.0. The main comparisons use seeds 0, 1, and 2, with the same seed set for every method. We evaluate the final checkpoint after the prescribed training budget. Training objective. For the main Aurora benchmark, we use weighted L1 loss on fields normalized with Auroras variable-specific statistics [4]. At each lead time, the surface term sums the variable-weighted spatial mean absolute errors and is multiplied by 1/4. The upper-air term averages spatial mean absolute errors over pressure levels and then takes weighted sum across variables. The combined loss is divided by the number of variable types, 3 + 5 = 8. The surface weights for (T 2M, 10, 10) are (3.0, 0.77, 0.66), and the upper-air weights for (Z, T, Q, U, ) are (3.0, 1.5, 0.6, 0.77, 0.54), shared across pressure levels. We average LST in Eq. Regional precipitation forecasting uses 10 epochs, an effective global batch size of 32, and learning rate of 3.75 104. Both settings use AdamW with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.999), weight decay 0.05, and cosine learning-rate schedule with one epoch of linear warmup. sections.title: F PROLA and Baseline Configurations
sections.content: For the main Aurora comparison, PROLA and all LoRA-style PEFT baselines fine-tune the linear projections in the backbones self-attention operations. All other pretrained backbone parameters remain frozen unless the method is Full FT. The spatial correction head Cs and temporal correction head Ct are trained in all methods in this comparison except where explicitly ablated. Thus, PEFT baseline comparisons use the same prediction pipeline and differ only in the backbone adaptation strategy. The default main comparison uses rank = 8 for all fixed-rank PEFT baselines. LoRA [13] uses the standard zero-output initialization. Unless otherwise stated, all adapters use no adapter dropout and do not train bias terms. DoRA [17] uses the same rank, target modules, dropout, and bias setting as LoRA, with the additional magnitude parameter trained following the original parameterization. PiSSA [14] initializes the low-rank factors from the top-r singular components of each pretrained weight and residualizes the frozen base weight to preserve the pretrained function at initialization. OPLoRA [15] uses fixed projectors onto the complements of the top-8 left and right singular subspaces of each pretrained weight, with the same trainable rank, target modules, dropout, and bias setting as LoRA. For PROLA, we use the same total low-rank budget = 8, split evenly into rp = 4 for the principal branch and ro = 4 for the orthogonal branch. The reference singular directions and orthogonal projectors are computed from the pretrained weights and kept fixed during adaptation, while the principal factors Ap, Bp remain trainable. We residualize the frozen base weight as in Eq. (9), set Bo,0 = 0, and sample the entries of Ao,0 from (0, σ2 o) with σo = 0.02, preserving the pretrained function. The complete PROLA configuration uses gradient-guided update scaling (Appendix B). With the principal branch removed (rp = 0, ro = 8), the orthogonal-only ablation retains fixed projectors onto the complements of each pretrained weights top-8 left and right singular subspaces. We set sg = α/rg for each PROLA branch {p, o} and = α/r for LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, and OPLoRA, with α = 1 for all five methods. AdaLoRA [18] uses α = 16, rinit = 12, rtarget = 8, mask updates every 10 optimizer steps, importance EMA coefficients β1 = β2 = 0.85, and orthogonal regularization weight 103. Initial and final warmups last one and two epochs of optimizer steps, respectively. Its target modules, dropout, and bias settings match the fixed-rank baselines. Head only trains Cs and Ct with the backbone frozen; Full FT also trains the backbone, using smaller learning rate for its pretrained weights. Table 6 reports the trainable-parameter counts for the main Aurora configuration. For PROLA, these comprise 2,850,816 backbone PEFT parameters (ϕPEFT), 831,856 temporal correction-head parameters (ϕt), and 236,828 spatial correction-head parameters (ϕs). Correction heads and numerical scaffolds. The correction heads Cs and Ct use separate surface and upper-air branches with hidden widths 32 and 512, respectively. Both use single depthwise 3 3 convolution followed by pointwise SwiGLU [57] projection, zero-initialized output projections, and no dropout. The spatial head Cs predicts terminal residual from the backbone forecast and endpoint conditioning fields. The temporal head Ct combines endpoint-conditioned residual basis maps using lead-dependent softmax gates. It uses 4 basis maps for surface variables and 12 for upper-air variables, with gate hidden widths 64 and 256 and 16-dimensional lead-time embedding. 20 Table 6: Trainable parameter counts for the main Aurora configuration. sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In Abstract and Introduction. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In the appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] 37 Justification: In the appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In Experiments and appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? 38 Answer: [Yes] Justification: We release the code. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In Experiments and appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We report mean and standard deviation over three seeds for the main comparisons. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In the appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We follow NeurIPS Code of Ethics. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In the appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. 40 The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: We do not release any datasets. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In the appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. 41 If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide code in the supplementary material. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve research with human subjects. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.
